fields.meta_title: Webinar Registration Form That Screens Sign-Ups | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a webinar registration form that screens each sign-up and sends confirmed registrants to your webinar platform. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Webinar Registration Form That Knows Who Signed Up
fields.hero_description: Describe who the session is for. Emergent builds the webinar registration form, checks every sign-up against your rules and keeps each answer in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Sits Behind a Webinar Sign-Up
fields.features_subheading: A name and an email take seconds to collect. The real work is deciding who gets the join link and where each answer goes next.
fields.feature_1:
Personal addresses flagged at entry

Ask for a work email and flag any address at gmail.com, yahoo.com or a domain you list. The registrant can fix it on the spot, or you let it through marked for a second look.
fields.feature_2:
Campaign source read from the link

Read utm_source and utm_campaign from the link each person clicked and store both on their row. A count by source shows whether the newsletter or a LinkedIn post filled the seats.
fields.feature_3:
Repeat sign-ups merged into one row

Someone who registers twice with one email updates their first row instead of adding a second. Your headcount stays accurate, and they get one confirmation with their latest answers.
fields.feature_4:
Approval before the join link goes out

Hold any registration that trips a rule you set, such as a domain missing from your customer list. An approver clears it from Slack or email, and only then is the confirmation sent.
fields.feature_5:
Sign-ups sent to your webinar platform

Push each confirmed sign-up through the API of the webinar platform you use, Zoom included, and store the join link it sends back. Answers to your own questions can sync to a CRM.
fields.feature_6:
The form's code in your repository

Export the code to GitHub whenever engineers want registration inside your product. Until then, publish on a custom domain, with the registrant table held in a database you own.

fields.usecase_heading: Sign-Up Rules for Four Kinds of Webinars
fields.tab_content_1:
Registrants from large companies go to a named rep

Pinecrest Analytics runs a monthly demo webinar, and its form asks each registrant for company size. Of 148 sign-ups for this month's demo, 37 work at companies of 200 or more. Each is assigned an account executive in HubSpot, who gets a Slack message with the registrant's answers before the demo.
fields.tab_content_2:
Certificates go only to people who stayed 50 minutes

Ridgeline Tax Society members sign up for its 60-minute tax update with their license number. Afterward, the app reads each attendee's minutes from the webinar platform's attendance report. Anyone who stayed 50 minutes or more gets an emailed certificate showing their license number. The rest get the recording.
fields.tab_content_3:
Only 263 of 420 names go to the partner

Ostrava Software is co-hosting a webinar with Brightwater Cloud. Its form carries one extra checkbox, left unticked by default: Share my details with Brightwater Cloud. Of 420 registrants, 263 ticked the box. The partner's export holds those 263 rows, and the other 157 stay in Ostrava's table alone.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every non-customer domain waits for one approver

Quarry Security holds a quarterly roadmap briefing for customers only. The form checks each registrant's email domain against the customer table, and a match is confirmed at once. Any other domain waits for Nadia Brooks in customer marketing. Nobody on that list gets a join link until she approves.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Webinar Registration Form
fields.howto_description: Work out who should end up on the attendee list before you write a single question.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide who the form should let in
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 List what each team needs to know
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write the consent line in plain words
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with the audience. A public demo can confirm anyone with a valid email, while a members' training or a customer briefing needs a check before anyone receives the link. That decision shapes most of the questions that follow.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Sales may want company size and role. An education team needs a license number for certificates. Ask every team that will use the list what it needs, then cut any question nobody will act on after the session.
fields.howto_step_3_des: If a co-host or sponsor will receive registrant details, say so on the form with a checkbox left empty. Name the company that gets the data. Registrants who skip the box stay on your list and nobody else's.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Write a prompt with the questions, the checks and where each answer should go. Emergent builds the form, the rules behind it and the registrant table. Change anything later by describing the change in another message.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Connect your webinar platform through its API so confirmed registrants are added and their join links come back. Connect HubSpot or another CRM the same way if sales follows up. Check that a sample registrant appears in both.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Test it as two different attendees
fields.howto_step_6_des: Sign up once with a personal address and once with a customer domain. Confirm the first is flagged and the second goes straight through, then look for both test rows in the table with every answer. Delete them before launch.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Publish and share the registration link
fields.howto_step_7_des: Publish the form on your own domain or embed it on the page that promotes the session. Add campaign tags to each link you share by email or on social media. The registrant table then shows which channel brought people in.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is a Google Form template, a Dribbble gallery, a help article on sending HubSpot form sign-ups to a webinar platform, a nonprofit's own sign-up page, pdfFiller templates, a software roundup, a hosted Jotform and a best-practices post; Semrush adds the Typeform, SurveyMonkey and Jotform galleries and the Zoom and Teams help pages. All of them treat the form as a list of fields. This page treats the webinar registration form as the gate in front of the attendee list: it checks who is signing up (company size, work email, customer domain), records consent to share details with a co-host, sends each approved registrant to the webinar platform through its API and keeps every answer in a table the host owns. The landing page itself, time zones, replays and reminders stay on the webinar landing page sibling; paid passes and breakouts stay on the conference sibling.
tab_stories: A Pinecrest Analytics demo webinar asks each registrant for company size, and anyone from a company of 200 or more is assigned an account executive in HubSpot, who gets a Slack message with the answers before the session.

The Ridgeline Tax Society collects license numbers on its tax update form, pulls the attendance report from Zoom after the hour, and emails a certificate only to the attendees who stayed at least 50 of the 60 minutes.

Ostrava Software co-hosts a webinar with Brightwater Cloud, and the form's unticked consent box decides whose details reach the partner: 263 of 420 registrants opted in, and only those rows are exported.

Quarry Security's customer roadmap briefing checks each registrant's email domain against its customer table, confirms matches at once and holds the rest for the customer marketing lead to approve before any join link goes out.
